body:
Why a network of exchange developed

The Harappan Civilisation was one of the earliest urban civilisations of the Indian subcontinent. During its Mature Harappan phase, approximately 2600–1900 BCE, settlements spread across the Indus region and adjoining areas, including present-day Gujarat, Rajasthan, Haryana, Punjab, Pakistan and parts of Afghanistan.

Harappan cities required regular supplies of food, raw materials and manufactured goods. Farmers and herders supplied agricultural produce, while craft specialists produced beads, ornaments, pottery, metal objects, seals and other articles. Because different materials were available in different geographical regions, exchange connected settlements that performed different economic activities.

Internal and external trade

Internal trade means the movement and exchange of goods between settlements within the Harappan civilisation. External trade means exchange with communities and regions beyond the Harappan cultural area, including parts of West Asia.

Internal trade connected villages, towns and cities

Harappan cities could not depend entirely on goods produced within their boundaries. Rural settlements supplied food, while distant regions supplied materials needed by urban workshops. For example, carnelian, a reddish semi-precious stone available around Bharuch in Gujarat, could be transported to centres where craftspeople manufactured beads. Finished beads could then move to other Harappan settlements or enter wider trading networks.

The same relationship applied to marine shells, metals and valuable stones. Some settlements were situated near sources of particular materials, while others became important centres of manufacture and exchange.

This system encouraged craft specialisation: certain settlements and craftspeople concentrated on producing particular goods. Chanhudaro was an important specialised craft centre, while Lothal combined craft production with access to coastal trade routes.

External exchange extended beyond the Indus region

Harappan goods also reached distant regions, particularly Mesopotamia, the Oman peninsula and the Persian Gulf. Contacts are indicated by objects of Harappan type discovered outside the civilisation and by references in Mesopotamian written records.

Finished ornaments, especially carnelian beads, were among the important goods associated with long-distance exchange. Timber, valuable stones and metals also circulated through these networks. Some goods may have passed through intermediate trading settlements rather than moving directly between their original producer and final consumer.

Exchange did not require modern currency

No established system of Harappan coinage is known. Exchange may have included direct exchange of goods, commonly called barter, as well as other arrangements that cannot now be reconstructed confidently.

The Harappans nevertheless possessed standardised stone weights, seals and methods of marking packages. These helped people measure goods and identify consignments. Since the Harappan script remains undeciphered, the precise rules governing prices, payments and commercial administration are not known.

The Harappan economy connected agricultural production, specialised manufacturing and long-distance exchange. Standardised weights and seals show organised commercial practices, but they do not establish the existence of coins or a modern monetary system.

Prelims focus

  • The Mature Harappan phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Internal trade connected Harappan villages, towns and cities.
  • External trade connected the Harappan region with West Asia, including Mesopotamia and Oman.
  • Carnelian from Gujarat was an important material for Harappan bead production.
  • Standardised weights and seals supported the exchange of goods.
  • Trap: The absence of known Harappan coinage does not mean that the Harappans lacked organised trade.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 1, 10–16; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, 'The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation', pp. 96–99; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 35–40.]

title: Trade and the Harappan Economy

body:
Land routes connected sources and settlements

Harappan trade depended on several forms of transport. Overland movement was important because many sources of raw materials were situated away from major rivers and coastal settlements.

Bullock carts were an important means of transporting goods and people over land. Terracotta models of carts with wheels provide evidence of wheeled transport. Such vehicles could move agricultural produce, pottery, stones and other goods between settlements.

Land connections also made it possible to obtain materials from regions such as Rajasthan, where copper was available, and areas farther northwest where valuable stones could be acquired.

Although the existence of wheeled transport is well supported, the exact roads followed by individual Harappan traders cannot generally be established.

River routes supported movement between settlements

The Indus and its tributaries formed an important geographical network within the Harappan region. Riverine transport means the movement of people or goods along rivers using boats and other watercraft.

River routes were probably used to move goods between settlements situated along connected waterways. They could complement land transport by providing another way to carry materials between production centres and urban settlements.

Evidence of boats in Harappan imagery supports the use of watercraft, although it does not establish the exact cargo or journey of every vessel.

Coastal routes connected the Harappans with distant regions

The Harappan civilisation extended to the Arabian Sea coast, including parts of Gujarat, Sindh and the Makran coast. Coastal settlements provided access to marine resources and opportunities for movement by water.

Lothal, near the Gulf of Khambhat in Gujarat, is particularly associated with maritime exchange. The presence of a large basin commonly identified as a dockyard, together with evidence of storage and craft production, makes it an important site for understanding coastal trade.

Harappan settlements on the Makran coast, including Sutkagen-dor and Sotka Koh, are associated with the civilisation's western coastal connections. Their precise functions in overseas trade remain open to interpretation.

Different routes served different purposes

Land, river and sea transport were complementary rather than competing systems. A material obtained from an inland source might first be carried by cart to a settlement, processed there and subsequently transported along a river or coast.

For example, carnelian obtained near Bharuch could be taken to a manufacturing centre such as Lothal. Finished beads could then be distributed within the Harappan region or become part of long-distance exchange.

The existence of several possible routes does not mean that every consignment passed through all 3 transport systems. The actual combination would have depended on geographical location, available transport and destination.

Archaeological evidence supports the use of land, river and maritime routes, but it does not provide a complete map of the exact journeys followed by Harappan merchants.

Prelims focus

  • Terracotta models of bullock carts provide evidence of wheeled land transport.
  • The Indus and its tributaries probably supported riverine movement.
  • The Arabian Sea coast provided access to maritime exchange.
  • Lothal in Gujarat is particularly associated with coastal trade.
  • Sutkagen-dor and Sotka Koh are associated with Harappan settlements on the Makran coast.
  • Trap: Every coastal Harappan settlement should not automatically be identified as a dockyard or major port.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', pp. 12–15 and Maps 1 and 3; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 37–40; George F. Dales, 'Harappan Outposts on the Makran Coast', Antiquity, abstract, consulted 17 November 2026.]

title: Moving Goods Across Land, Rivers and Coasts

body:
Standard weights made exchange more consistent

People exchanging goods need a way to determine how much material is being transferred. The Harappans developed a remarkably standardised system of weights, which helped make measured quantities comparable across settlements.

Harappan weights were usually made of chert, a hard stone. They were generally cubical and unmarked. Their sizes and masses followed recognised patterns, allowing different combinations of weights to be used.

The lower denominations followed a binary progression, in which successive values commonly doubled:

1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64

Higher denominations also incorporated a decimal system, using larger multiples of standard values. Thus, the Harappan weight system combined binary and decimal principles rather than following a single simple sequence at every level.

The numbers in the progression represent relative weight denominations. They should not be mistaken for gram values.

Smaller weights were probably used for valuable goods such as jewellery and beads. Metal scale-pans have also been discovered, supporting the interpretation that goods were weighed rather than assessed only by appearance or volume.

Weights and measures are related but different

Weights were used to compare quantities of material by mass. Measures of length were relevant to activities such as construction and craft production.

Harappan bricks commonly followed standard proportions, showing the importance of consistent dimensions. A graduated ivory object found at Lothal has also been studied as a possible measuring scale. However, the precise Harappan system of length units is less securely established than its system of stone weights.

Standardisation helped people working in different settlements produce comparable objects and exchange measured quantities. It does not, by itself, reveal the exact organisation of trade or the identity of those who controlled it.

Seals identified goods and consignments

Harappan seals were commonly made of steatite, a relatively soft stone that could be worked and hardened. Many seals show an animal motif together with a short inscription in the Harappan script.

The script remains undeciphered. It is therefore not possible to read the names, titles or commercial messages that may have appeared on particular seals with certainty.

Seals are especially important because they could be pressed into wet clay to create impressions used in identifying or securing consignments of goods.

How a sealing could protect a package

A package or bag containing goods could be closed and tied with a rope. Wet clay was then applied over the knot, and a seal was pressed into it. The resulting clay impression was called a sealing.

If the sealing remained intact when the package arrived, the recipient could reasonably conclude that the fastening had not been opened after sealing. The impression could also help identify the sender or another party associated with the consignment.

Seal and sealing are not the same object

A seal is the object used to make an impression. A sealing is the impression left on clay or another suitable material. A sealing could help indicate whether a package had been opened.

Seals and sealings provide evidence of organised exchange and communication. They should not be confused with coins, nor can their undeciphered inscriptions be treated as readable commercial accounts.

Prelims focus

  • Harappan weights were generally cubical and commonly made of chert.
  • Smaller weight denominations followed a binary progression such as 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64.
  • Higher weight denominations incorporated decimal multiples.
  • Metal scale-pans have been found at Harappan sites.
  • Harappan seals were commonly made of steatite, and their script remains undeciphered.
  • Trap: A seal is the stamping object; a sealing is its impression.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', Sections 7.1–7.3, pp. 15–16; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 36 and 40; Michel Danino, 'Issues in Indian Metrology, from Harappa to Bhaskaracharya', Ganita Bharati, Vol. 37, 2015, pp. 129–130, consulted 17 November 2026 through the IIT Gandhinagar archive.]

title: Weights, Measures, Seals and Sealings

body:
Production depended on materials from different regions

Harappan craftspeople used stone, metal, shell, clay, wood and other materials to manufacture objects for everyday use and exchange. Some materials were available locally, but others had to be obtained from distant regions.

A useful distinction is between a raw material, which is obtained before manufacture, and a finished product, which has been processed into a usable article.

For example, a piece of carnelian obtained from a stone-bearing region was a raw material. A polished and drilled carnelian bead was a finished product. The bead could be used as an ornament or exchanged with another settlement.

Important materials and their sources

MaterialImportant source or connectionUse or trade significance
CarnelianBharuch region, GujaratSemi-precious stone used for beads and ornaments.
SteatiteNorth Gujarat and southern RajasthanUsed for seals and beads.
Marine shellCoastal areas, including Nageshwar and BalakotUsed for bangles, ladles and decorative inlay.
CopperKhetri region of Rajasthan; probably also OmanUsed for tools, vessels and ornaments.
TinPossibly Afghanistan and IranCombined with copper to produce bronze.
Lapis lazuliSources in northeastern Afghanistan, near ShortughaiValuable blue stone used for ornaments and exchange.
GoldPossibly southern India, including present-day KarnatakaUsed for valuable ornaments and other articles.

The sources listed for copper, tin and gold are possible or probable connections, not evidence that every piece of metal followed the same route. The Harappans could obtain materials through exchange with neighbouring communities as well as through longer-distance contacts.

Important centres of craft production

Chanhudaro

Chanhudaro was an important centre of specialised manufacture. Its crafts included bead-making, shell-working, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making.

Lothal

Lothal in Gujarat was an important centre for working stone, shell and metal. Evidence of bead production includes raw materials, unfinished beads, tools and finished objects. Its position near the Gulf of Khambhat also gave it access to coastal exchange.

Nageshwar and Balakot

These coastal settlements were particularly associated with shell-working. Shell objects such as bangles and decorative pieces could be transported to other Harappan settlements.

Shortughai

Shortughai, in present-day Afghanistan, was situated near important sources of lapis lazuli. It illustrates how Harappan connections extended far beyond the principal urban settlements of the Indus plain.

How carnelian became an exchangeable product

Carnelian was especially important in Harappan ornament production. Craftspeople selected suitable stone, shaped it, ground and polished it, and drilled holes to make beads. Heating was also used in producing the characteristic reddish colour.

Specialised drills associated with bead manufacture have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and Dholavira.

Once finished, beads could move from manufacturing centres to larger urban settlements such as Harappa or Mohenjodaro. Some also became part of the external exchange network.

A place where a valuable commodity was manufactured was not necessarily the place where its raw material originated. Similarly, a commodity traded through the Harappan region need not have been produced entirely within that region.

Prelims focus

  • Carnelian: important sources near Bharuch in Gujarat; used for beads.
  • Chanhudaro: important specialised craft-production centre.
  • Lothal: significant bead-making and craft centre in Gujarat.
  • Nageshwar and Balakot: associated with shell-working.
  • Shortughai: Harappan settlement in Afghanistan near lapis lazuli sources.
  • Trap: Shortughai was associated with obtaining valuable stone, not with a Gujarat coastal port.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, 'Bricks, Beads and Bones', Sections 5, 6.1 and 6.2, pp. 10–15; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, 'In the Earliest Cities', pp. 36–40; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 2, 'Arts of the Indus Valley', pp. 13–14.]
